subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal agenesis, solitary kidney, multicystic dysplastic kidney
vignette: A prenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks identifies a single kidney in the right renal fossa. On the left there is no renal tissue and no ureter is visualized. The infant is born with a solitary left-sided functioning kidney, and the left kidney later shows compensatory enlargement.
question: Which embryologic event most likely produced this picture of unilateral renal agenesis?

options.text: Failure of the ureteric bud to develop and induce the metanephric mesenchyme
Ureteric bud develops but fails to induce the metanephric mesenchyme
Failure of the mesonephros to function in the first trimester
Incomplete canalization of the ureteropelvic junction
Fusion of the inferior poles of the two kidneys

explanation_correct: In unilateral renal agenesis, the ureteric bud fails to develop and therefore cannot induce differentiation of the metanephric mesenchyme, producing complete absence of both the kidney and its ureter. This matches the absent left kidney and absent ureter, with compensatory changes in the surviving kidney. Bilateral agenesis would instead lead to Potter sequence from absent fetal urine output.

explanation_incorrect.B: A ureteric bud that develops but fails to induce the mesenchyme produces a multicystic dysplastic kidney, not agenesis; a ureter and a nonfunctional cystic renal remnant would be present.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mesonephros function in the first trimester is unrelated to formation of the permanent kidney; its failure would not cause absence of the kidney and ureter.
explanation_incorrect.D: Incomplete canalization of the ureteropelvic junction causes congenital hydronephrosis, not absence of the kidney and ureter.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fusion of the inferior poles produces a horseshoe kidney, in which two kidneys are present and fused rather than one being absent.

educationalObjective: Unilateral renal agenesis results from failure of the ureteric bud to develop, causing complete absence of the kidney and ureter.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal agenesis, solitary kidney, multicystic dysplastic kidney
vignette: An infant is evaluated for a palpable left flank mass. Imaging shows a nonfunctional renal structure composed of multiple cysts separated by connective tissue, with an identifiable ureter draining it. The contralateral kidney is normal and hypertrophied. There is no family history of a defined genetic syndrome.
question: Which embryologic abnormality best explains this multicystic dysplastic kidney?

options.text: The ureteric bud fails to develop at all
The ureteric bud bifurcates before reaching the blastema
The inferior poles of both kidneys fuse and are trapped
The ureteropelvic junction fails to canalize
The ureteric bud develops but fails to induce differentiation of the metanephric mesenchyme

explanation_correct: In multicystic dysplastic kidney, the ureteric bud develops but fails to induce differentiation of the metanephric mesenchyme, leaving a nonfunctional kidney made of cysts and connective tissue. It is usually unilateral and has a nongenetic inheritance pattern, though it tends to run in families. The presence of a ureter distinguishes it from agenesis, in which the bud never forms.

explanation_incorrect.A: Failure of the ureteric bud to develop produces renal agenesis with absence of the kidney and ureter, not a cystic renal remnant with a ureter.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bifurcation of the ureteric bud before it reaches the blastema produces a duplex collecting system with a bifid ureter, not a multicystic dysplastic kidney.
explanation_incorrect.C: Fusion of the inferior poles with entrapment under the inferior mesenteric artery describes a horseshoe kidney, not a dysplastic cystic kidney.
explanation_incorrect.D: Failure of ureteropelvic junction canalization causes hydronephrosis of an otherwise formed kidney, not a nonfunctional cystic and connective-tissue mass.

educationalObjective: Multicystic dysplastic kidney results when the ureteric bud forms but fails to induce the metanephric mesenchyme, producing a unilateral nonfunctional cystic kidney.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal agenesis, solitary kidney, multicystic dysplastic kidney
vignette: A 7-year-old is found on a school screening ultrasound to have a single kidney. The child is asymptomatic with normal blood pressure, normal serum creatinine, and no edema. The remaining kidney is enlarged for the child's age, and further imaging confirms absence of the other kidney. The pediatrician discusses expected long-term adaptations.
question: Which of the following is most likely in a child with a congenital solitary functioning kidney?

options.text: Progressive renal failure in early childhood in essentially all cases
Atrophy of the remaining kidney from underuse
Compensatory hypertrophy of the remaining kidney
Development of Potter sequence after birth
Obligatory occurrence of ureteropelvic junction obstruction

explanation_correct: Most children with a congenital solitary functioning kidney are asymptomatic and show compensatory hypertrophy of the remaining kidney. Anomalies of the contralateral or solitary kidney are common, and the condition is often diagnosed prenatally by ultrasound. Bilateral agenesis or severe dysplasia, not a single functioning kidney, is what leads to Potter sequence.

explanation_incorrect.A: The majority of affected children are asymptomatic; progressive renal failure in early childhood in essentially all cases is not the expected course.
explanation_incorrect.B: The remaining kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy rather than atrophy; a single working kidney increases its workload and nephron size.
explanation_incorrect.D: Potter sequence results from bilateral agenesis or dysplasia with absent fetal urine output, not from having one normal functioning kidney.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is not obligatory in a solitary kidney; it is a separate congenital anomaly that can occur but is not a defining consequence.

educationalObjective: A congenital solitary functioning kidney is usually asymptomatic and shows compensatory hypertrophy, though anomalies of the remaining kidney are common.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal agenesis, solitary kidney, multicystic dysplastic kidney
vignette: A counselor is explaining the features of multicystic dysplastic kidney to a family whose newborn was diagnosed with the condition. The kidney was nonfunctional and removed, and the parents ask whether this reflects an inherited genetic syndrome and whether both kidneys are typically involved.
question: Which of the following statements about multicystic dysplastic kidney is correct?

options.text: It is always bilateral and uniformly fatal in the neonatal period
It is usually unilateral and has nongenetic inheritance, though it tends to run in families
It results from complete failure of the ureteric bud to form
It is a functional kidney that simply has a few incidental simple cysts
It is caused by fusion of the inferior poles beneath the inferior mesenteric artery

explanation_correct: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is usually unilateral and follows nongenetic inheritance, though it tends to run in families. It is a nonfunctional kidney composed of cysts and connective tissue that results when the ureteric bud develops but fails to induce the metanephric mesenchyme. The contralateral kidney is typically normal and compensates.

explanation_incorrect.A: It is usually unilateral, not always bilateral; bilateral severe involvement can lead to Potter sequence, but the classic lesion is a unilateral nonfunctional kidney.
explanation_incorrect.C: Complete failure of the ureteric bud to form causes renal agenesis with absence of the kidney and ureter, not a multicystic dysplastic kidney.
explanation_incorrect.D: The kidney is nonfunctional and dysplastic, with cysts and connective tissue, rather than a normal kidney with a few simple cysts.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fusion of the inferior poles beneath the inferior mesenteric artery is the mechanism of a horseshoe kidney, not of multicystic dysplastic kidney.

educationalObjective: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is usually unilateral, nongenetic but familial-appearing, and nonfunctional, consisting of cysts and connective tissue.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal agenesis, solitary kidney, multicystic dysplastic kidney
vignette: Two newborns each have a nonfunctioning kidney on one side. In the first infant, imaging shows no renal tissue and no ureter on the affected side. In the second, a cystic renal mass is present and a thin ureter can be traced to it. The clinicians wish to distinguish unilateral renal agenesis from multicystic dysplastic kidney on an embryologic basis.
question: Which finding best distinguishes unilateral renal agenesis from multicystic dysplastic kidney?

options.text: Whether the condition is unilateral or bilateral
The presence of cysts and connective tissue in the renal remnant
Whether compensatory hypertrophy of the contralateral kidney occurs
Presence of a ureter on the affected side
A tendency to run in families

explanation_correct: The key discriminating feature is whether a ureter is present. In renal agenesis the ureteric bud fails to develop, so both kidney and ureter are absent. In multicystic dysplastic kidney the ureteric bud does develop but fails to induce the mesenchyme, so a ureter is present along with a nonfunctional cystic remnant. Both conditions are usually unilateral, both can show contralateral compensatory hypertrophy, and MCDK can appear familial.

explanation_incorrect.A: Both renal agenesis and multicystic dysplastic kidney are usually unilateral, so laterality does not reliably distinguish them.
explanation_incorrect.B: Cysts and connective tissue identify a multicystic dysplastic kidney when a remnant is present, but agenesis has no remnant at all; the more fundamental embryologic distinction rests on whether the ureter formed.
explanation_incorrect.C: Both conditions leave the contralateral kidney to compensate, so hypertrophy of the normal kidney does not separate agenesis from dysplasia.
explanation_incorrect.E: A familial tendency is described for multicystic dysplastic kidney, but it is a nongenetic pattern and is not the defining difference from agenesis.

educationalObjective: A present ureter indicates multicystic dysplastic kidney (bud formed, induction failed); an absent ureter indicates renal agenesis (bud never formed).
